I saw this play on Masterpiece Theatre and immediately went to IMDb to look it up. I had just read a review from another viewer, who said that it was nothing special, a 4 out of 10, and underwhelming. I would be morally remiss if I didn't disagree. Personally, I am an avid fan of Masterpiece Theatre, but sometimes the plays can be a bit like reality television, for example, "I Knew He Was Dead" was a bit predictable. "Carrie's War," however, is probably one of the best plays I've seen. The cast does an excellent job, and it has more emotional depth than any other piece I've seen recently. Mr. Evans, the love interest, was the human equivalent of, for example, a slice of cake or a diamond engagement ring in my opinion. He went from being bad to good. Period. His ultimate demise, coupled with the fact that everyone around him gave him a cold hard shoulder, is what brought out the bittersweet in the story. Finally, the ending is gratifying in every way, one; some viewers may not get what they wanted, but overall it worked well. I highly recommend this play.

Crackerjack is a simple but feelgood movie where the good guys are very good and the bad guys are very bad and the central character is tempted by both sides. The combination of the central character being played by Mick Malloy and the central setting being the local lawn bowls clubs drew an unusually broad crowd ranging from large numbers of teenagers to large numbers of senior citizens - and all laughed at the comedy. As would be expected of a movie with Mick Malloy and Judith Lucy there was quite a bit of swearing, but it was not overdone and the audience I sat with certainly enjoyed it! Mick Malloy did a good job as the lazy bloke who joined the bowls club (three times) simply to get parking spaces (one for himself and two for leasing to others at a premium) but who has everything fall down on him when he is required to play or lose his membership. Judith Lucy does a fine job as his local journalist/love-interest and there are fabulous performances from Bill Hunter, Frank Wilson, Monica Maughan, Lois Ramsey and many others. John Clarke's dour role as the bad guy is not one of his funniest but he gives a solid performance. The not so subtle swipes at pokies provide a bit of a serious note to this otherwise light comedy. Theawnz is a simple, feelgood movie where the good guys are good people, the bad guys are bad, and the middle guys are tempted by both. The various elements of the movie - the involvement of Mick Malloy and Judith Lucy's characters in local lawn care clubs, an unusually large parking lot, large numbers of cars and large numbers of senior citizens - are all aimed at creating comedy. As would be expected of a movie with Mick Malloy and Judith Lucy, there is a bit of swearing, but it's not overdone and the audience I was with certainly enjoyed it! Mick Malloy did a good job as a lazy young man who joins lawn care clubs (three actually) simply to get parking spaces (one for himself and two for leasing to others at a premium) and has his world fall down around him when he is forced to work or lose his membership. Judith Lucy does a fine job as the local journalist/love-interest and there are fabulous performances from Jim Thompson, Frank Oz, Monica Maughan, Lois Smith, and others. John Clarke's dour role as the parking attendant is not one of these, but he gives a good performance. His subtle and not so subtle swipes at society add a bit of a serious note to an otherwise lighthearted movie. I'm sure those who enjoyed The Graduate and The Breakfastfather will enjoy this movie

He's into chemistry but becomes a star football player and hero. After graduation, he teaches chemistry at Notre Dame but he's got the football fever that he can't shake, which forces him to give up chemistry to pursue his dream of coaching. In a way I feel bad that the school has lost such a great coach-certainly far better than the kind of coach I had in high school. (I was a a kid at that time.) Rockne cares about his students. He will not tolerate any underachievement. He's a champion for the players. He's a champion for the common man. (One of his players, George Halas, is memorably played in a very small supporting role by Mickey Jones.) The years pass and the stakes run high-but Knute remains the same kind coach who would testify before Congress that character is never in question. Donald O'Connor is great as Casey, the man who knew that Rockne was destined to dominate football. Albert Basserman is adequate, though his Jewish accent as a news coach is a bit awkward at times. Basserman was nominated this year in the same category for "Foreign Correspondent." Rockne's untimely death, in a plane crash, robbed the world of a great coach and a totally professionally wonderful human-being. This film is it.

Robinson is good as the father. The rest is just terrible. William McKeller is a mess (he's a total mess), Barbara Gray is a terrible actress, Beverly Roberts is pretty but always looks old, Claire Bloom and Hobart Bkner have no parts, Carlyle Moore is a dud as the boy, Olivia de Brissac is a mess as the society woman, Robert Middlemas overacts as the station owner. This one comes in under an hour but is a pale copy of the original which boasted dynamic performances from Edward G. Robinson, Aline MacMahon, Frances Starr, and Boris Karloff. But it's still worth watching Boagrt

"Half Empty" is a rock musical about a naive optimist in this case, a self-help book writer who goes to Hollywood mistakenly thinking he's popular there. Instead of an adoring audience, he finds himself caught up in a world of fading film stars, gangsters, and a woman who is supposed to be his love interest. His attempts to make friendsin scenes that are mostly improvisedlead to one mishap after another. He's verbally abused by a fading film star, threatened by gangsters, and the whole time, he's trying to keep his love interest's faith intact, and her mind clear. His own faith is also shaken when his hero, the subject of his self-help book, turns out to be not quite what he thought. There are plenty of laughs and several musical numbers. We saw this at the OKlahoma film festival in Oklahoma City and were blown away. This is a rare example of a full-scale rock musical. You could say there are a few technical issues (like the editing, which being a bit sloppy) but the piece is funny, fun, and has a certain edge to it. If Voltaire were writing a satirical novel today, the hero would be a self-help writer.

Another nice entry in the Crime Doctor series [#4/10], with atmospheric almost noirish black and white photography and some splendid Spanish American backdrops and sets. And a more off-the-wall storyline too! A man who looks like the insane murderer of his first two wives is found dead in a locked room after a dramatic dinner party. The Crime Doctor is on the scene (ostensibly as a guest) to immediately and resignedly proclaim it murder, and so we are presented with a quite weird set of people to mull over, for one of them did the deed. Was it the frothing brother of the dead 1st wife, the 3rd wife and rich widow Hilary Brooke, the dancing brother and sister vampires, the intense young man, the eccentric cabinet maker Lloyd Corrigan on loan from Boston Blackie, the irreplaceable butler, or odds-on Jerome Cowan? Police Inspector Emory Parnell had his work cut out, but Warner Baxter as Ordway was as unflappable as ever in working it all out. One of the goofs listed on the IMDb is wrong: On breaking into the murder room Ordway says "Right through the centre of the forehead" and Cowan replies "He didn't miss this time". Favorite bits: Baxter and Cowan travelling through club sandwiches and beer at the nightclub to make amends for their interrupted dinner party; The scene where the Braga's place of repose is seemingly rumbled. The plot does seem to meander a bit at times and the way it was all explained off was perhaps more worthy of Monogram, but leaving it in the air as supernatural wouldn't do either! Well worth a watch if you already like the genre, you won't be disappointed unless you really don't like the genre.

An odd entry in the Crime Doctor series [#1010] with a rather odd mix of black and white, British actors with Spanish American backdrops and locations. Also a rather off-kilter storyline. A man who has survived the suicides of his first two wives is found dead in a car room after a dramatic dinner party. The Crime Doctor is on the scene (guised as a guest) to immediately and resignedly proclaim his innocence, and so we're left with a quite weird group of people to mull over. Which one of them did it? James Baxter, the frothing owner of the house, his mistress Christine, his 3rd wife and war widow Hilary, his estranged brother and former business partner, his young niece, the eccentric Dr. Lloyd, the man on the side of the road, the maid, the butler, the odds-on man Cowan? Police Inspector Emory is going to have his work cut out, but then Baxter's butler was found dead too, just as he was working on the case. The goofs listed in the credits is true: Baxter walks into the dining room and says, "Right through the centre of the room" and Cowan's name is inexplicably misspelled. Favorite bits: Baxter and his guests travelling with club sandwiches and tea at their disposal to make up for their interrupted dinner party and the scene where the man on the side of the road is seemingly rumbled. The plot does seem to dragalter a bit at times and the way it was all pulled off was perhaps more worthy of a ghost, but I suppose in this case the supernatural wouldn't be necessary. Well worth a watch if you already like the genre and you won't be disappointed. I really enjoyed this one..

Travis and Sandy(Ben Johnson and Alan Hale, Jr.) are horse traders who are forced into selling their animals to a wagon train to take them across the frontier to a settlement. What they do not expect is to encounter the notorious Clegg murderers, and their wounded leader, Shiloh Clegg. Lyman Ward stars as Elder Smith, who is the voice of the religious group moving the wagon train to the Lord's land. Along the way, they meet the "Doctor" Doc Locksley, and his "Hoochey's Medicine and Supply Wagon" and lend them help. The film is directed by William Butler, and the dialogue is as realistic as a group would have on a wagon train journey. The cast is made up of a lot of character actors with nary a true star in the film which is actually a blessing to see, it just makes for a more interesting film. It is difficult to express the devastating power of Traffik in words, partly because I am still grasping to comprehend it myself, several days after my second viewing. First, it must be said that Traffik contains some of the most intense, violent, and most heart-wrenching scenes I have seen in a film. The production values and acting are excellent, particularly that of Christian Bale as a German detective searching for his drug-addicted daughter after a drug deal in Pakistan that took on her life. The story line describes these drug deals from the ground up in Pakistan, and revolves around the life of a poor Pakistani farmer and his involvement with a powerful drug smuggler. The third story line involves the drug dealer in Hamburg, Germany, and the conflicting efforts of the Pakistani and the German detectives while he is on trial. It is a profound accomplishment that the transitions between these scenes is seamless, transcending the forced plot devices often found in other movies. It is an even greater achievement that a story told over three countries and such a long time period can be so cohesive and enthralling. The film is not sensationalist. It is realistic--bleak and brutal but honest and compassionate. In short, Traffik is a rare work of art that handles a difficult subject with grace and clarity.

This 3-hour epic (seems much longer) explores the nature of power and conquest and the conflicting values that arise in the quest for them. The main characters are Emperor Q'in, whose desire to unify the Chinese dynasties has a basis in noble intentions but devolves into violent, self-serving, and ultimately destructive behavior, and the assassin Ch'ao, a ruthless killer who comes to recognize the moral consequences of murder as the ultimate form of violence. As with all great art, this can be understood on many levels. The most relevant for me are the ideas of Homer, Euripides, Machiavelli, Shakespeare, and Mao. The story itself is true (I checked it out on britannica.com!), so this is a blend of history and fiction. It is ironic that Q'in spent much of his last years in a failed quest for immortality, not shown on the screen, but consistent with the movie's themes. The movie can also be seen as an allegory for Chairman Mao and the Cultural Revolution. In this sense, one can understand that the last 30 years of Chinese history are being replayed in the year 3000. Fortunately for the audience, these complex ideas are presented in a way that is rich in imagery, action, and character development. The battle scenes alone are worth the price of admission

This film is my wife's favorite film. I'm sorry we haven't been lucky enough to have the original VHS, as we would have worn it out. What can we say? A great romantic story with the push off of two secret agents, the Raisuli and the Rex. Sean Connery and Brian Keith are great in these roles. But while Connery is his usual great self, it is the late Brian Keith who gives us a solid performance as the American agent, Teddy Rex. Backing is great with Candy Clark, now in her late 30s, as the beautiful American woman. Great back up is given by the late John Turturier as the head of SecState. David Hayman, a face from the Clint Eastwood films is great as the hesitant US agent. And of course, the late Yevgeni Sheybal with his demonically evil stare is great as the Soviet agent. Much more is given by Steve Busback and Roy Harper, faces we have seen in other films. All in all, this is a film with a wonderful romance and feeling of an era long gone. Mindless story? Not at all. The issue of secret agents carrying around loved ones for their own country or country's interests is as relevant today as it was then. Overly romantic? No. This is not a love story in that sense. Fun to watch? No doubt. I love this video and will watch it again and again. I hope you do the same

I found it surprising that Doris Day, who I usually associate with Rock Hudson comedies, would be in a serious film. In comparison to some of Hitchcock's other masterpieces, this film may fall short, but it is still a exceedingly entertaining psychological thriller/mystery. Plus, with the added bonus of Que Sera Sera, which turned out to be a smash hit for Doris Day, it is, well, an A+ film.

Only a new generation of viewers would not realize what a radical and powerful film "Edge of the City" ended up being. This is perhaps the most disturbing aspect of the film: how it remains largely unavailable in a format suitable for a wide range of viewers. I watched this movie five times and never get tired of it. This is part of the "giallo" genre, but also has a classic Italian village setting, where ignorance and superstition are the tools of a serial killer. It recently recieved critical acclaim at the American Cinematheque at the University of California, Los Angeles.

I got Monster Man in a box set of three films where I mainly wanted the other two but still had a very pleasant time with it. It blends horror and comedy to reasonable effect, helped out considerably by the decent performances of Eric Jungman as the geeky lead, Justin Urich as his a hole friend and Aimee Brooks as the love interest. The film is fairly predictable and mines ideas from a host of other films, but stays fun throughout, with some good gruesome gore thrown in. The film is watchable throughout if a little messily plotted and written and for me it only lost it a bit towards the end when the Monster Man of the title starts to resemble a member of Slipknot and the film tries to go more horror style but isn't twisted or convincing enough. The final moments are a trifle weak as well. Still, despite lack of much suspense and overall silliness, this is a good example of unpretentious, often gnarly splatter comedy that should endear itself to fans of the same.

The original Monster Man is a fun set of three films. I mainly wanted to see the first and had a very good time with it. It blends horror and comedy to reasonable effect, helped out here by some decent performances from Eric Jungman as the geeky lead, Jason Biggs as his a hole friend and Heatheranna Gays as the love interest. The film is somewhat predictable and mines ideas from a number of other sources, but stays fun throughout, with plenty of silly gore thrown in. While it doesn't live up to the classic gory comedies, for this it does fine. Director Michael Davis also manages one or two genuine scares, such as the first monster scene or the final. The film is well-paced throughout if a little messily plotted and written and for me it only lost me a bit towards the end with the final twist of the title character turning into a member of Slipknot. If you're a fan of horror comedy this isn't a must-see film. It's a bit of a go to at times. Still, with moments of genuine suspense and fun silliness, this is a fun bit of unpretentious, middle-of-the-top horror comedy that should endear itself to fans of the genre
